bayome

BAYesian Occurrence–abundance Microbiome Estimation

bayome finds associations between microbial features (taxa, genes, pathways) and sample metadata. For each feature it models the occurrence (presence/absence) and the abundance together, links the abundance effects to the occurrence effects, and shares information across features, so that features with few observations still get stable estimates and honest intervals. Every model is fitted with the integrated nested Laplace approximation (R-INLA).

The arguments, formulas and output columns follow MaAsLin3, so an existing MaAsLin3 analysis runs by changing only the function name.

Website and worked example: https://jmartinez-minaya.github.io/bayome/

Status: early development (version 0.0.0.9000). The default model (shrinkage = "joint") and the default selection rule (selection = "bh_lfsr") work and are tested on simulated data, not yet on real data.

Installation

INLA is not on CRAN. Install it first:

install.packages(
  "INLA",
  repos = c(getOption("repos"),
            INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"),
  dep = TRUE
)

Then install bayome from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("jmartinez-minaya/bayome")

Quick start 

library(bayome)

fit <- bayome(
  input_data     = taxa,      # samples x features (or features x samples)
  input_metadata = meta,      # samples in rows
  output         = "bayome_output",
  formula        = ~ diagnosis + age + (1 | subject),
  exposure       = "diagnosis", # variable of interest; age is an adjustment
  reference      = "diagnosis,nonIBD"
)

fit
head(fit$results)

output gets all_results.tsv and significant_results.tsv. Use output = NULL to keep the results in R only.

Plots (ggplot2 objects):

bm_plot_summary(fit)                              # top features, all coefficients
bm_plot_effects(fit, "diagnosisCD")               # effects with credible intervals
bm_plot_link(fit, "diagnosisCD")                  # prevalence vs abundance effects
bm_plot_association(fit, "Faecalibacterium_prausnitzii", "diagnosis")  # the data

The vignette (“Getting started with bayome”) runs the whole workflow on the HMP2 inflammatory bowel disease data included in the package.

The model

For each feature j and sample i, with Yij the normalised abundance:

  • Prevalence (all samples): logit P(Yij > 0) = xi’ βjprev + random effects
  • Abundance (samples where the feature is present): log2Yij = xi’ βjabun + random effects + εij

Both parts are fitted together in one INLA call, with a binomial and a Gaussian likelihood. Pre-processing: normalise (TSS, CLR or NONE), filter, then transform (LOG, PLOG or NONE). Continuous covariates are standardised by default.

The default model (shrinkage = "joint")

All features and both parts go into one INLA model. The model distinguishes the exposure (exposure = "diagnosis": the variable of interest; by default the first variable of the formula) from the adjustment covariates (all the others). For an exposure coefficient k (for example diagnosisCD), the effect on feature j is split as:

  • Prevalence: βjkP = μkP + ujkP, with ujkP ~ N(0, 2.5²) fixed: each feature is estimated from its own presence data, without pooling.
  • Abundance: βjkA = μkA + λk · ujkP + ejk, with ejk ~ N(0, 1/τk) shared across features.

λk is one number per exposure coefficient, estimated from all features: how much abundance tends to follow prevalence in these data. A feature with few non-zero samples has its abundance effect shrunk towards what its prevalence effect suggests, instead of towards zero. When prevalence and abundance are unrelated, λk ≈ 0 and the model reduces to an independent hierarchical abundance model.

Each adjustment covariate l (for example age or antibiotic use) gets one effect per feature and part, γjl ~ N(0, 2.5²) with a fixed prior: no pooling, no link and no extra hyperparameters. So the model has two hyperparameters per exposure coefficient (λk and τk) plus the variances of the random effects, however many adjustment covariates there are. To give every covariate the full structure, list them all in exposure.

Random effects of the formula (for example (1 | subject)) get one copy per part, replicated per feature with a shared variance. Residual variances are one per feature, estimated with "vb" (variational updates with a common prior). The abundance effects are compared with their median over features (compositional correction). The estimated λ values are printed during the fit and stored in fit$lambda.

The alternatives are shrinkage = "hierarchical" (each part separately, with a common prior for each) and shrinkage = "none" (each feature on its own).

Priors are set with bm_prior():

Component Default prior
Fixed effects, prevalence Normal(0, 2.5²) on the log-odds scale
Fixed effects, abundance Normal(0, 10²) on the log2 scale
Random-effect SDs PC prior, P(σ > 1) = 0.01
ordered() random walk PC prior, P(σ > 1) = 0.01
Between-feature SD ("joint": abundance e; "hierarchical": both parts) PC prior, P(σ > 1) = 0.01 (set with bm_prior(random = ))
Prevalence effect per feature uP ("joint") Normal(0, 2.5²), fixed (no pooling; set with bm_prior(fixed_sd_prevalence = ))
Prevalence–abundance link λ ("joint") Normal(0, 1)
Adjustment covariate effect per feature γ ("joint") Normal(0, 2.5²), fixed, both parts (set with bm_prior(adjustment_sd = ))
strata() iid effect with fixed, very small precision

Compositional correction

With relative abundances (TSS), when some features truly increase, all the others appear to decrease. Each abundance coefficient is therefore compared with the median of that coefficient across features instead of with zero (median_comparison_abundance = TRUE, the default).

bayome does this on the posterior. For each coefficient and posterior draw s:

  • m(s) = median over features j of βj(s)
  • δj(s) = βj(s) − m(s)

lfsr, prob_positive and the q-values then refer to δ, whose posterior includes the uncertainty of the median. coef keeps the raw coefficient unless subtract_median = TRUE. null_hypothesis reports the median used. Draws are random: call set.seed() first for reproducible results.

Sharing information across features

shrinkage Prevalence Abundance Link between parts
"joint" (default) Each feature on its own (fixed N(0, 2.5²) prior) Common prior across features, centred on λ·uP λ per covariate
"hierarchical" Common prior across features, centred at 0 Common prior across features (hierarchical_reference: μ or median) None
"none" Each feature on its own Each feature on its own None (or shared random intercepts with link = "shared")

With "hierarchical", hierarchical_variance sets the residual variances ("vb" by default, "plugin" from an lm() per feature, or "estimated" inside INLA, which is much slower).

Formula notation

Formulas are written in lme4-style notation and translated into INLA internally. bm_inla_formula() shows the result of the translation.

You write Meaning INLA term
diagnosis + age Fixed effects unchanged
group(site) Categorical variable tested as a whole fixed factor (joint inference: planned)
ordered(stage) Ordered categorical; each level is compared with the previous one f(stage, model = "rw1") (only with shrinkage = "none")
strata(pair) Matched designs (only one allowed) f(pair, model = "iid") with fixed small precision
(1 \| subject) Random intercept f(subject, model = "iid")
(age \|\| subject) Uncorrelated random intercept and slope two iid terms
(age \| subject) Correlated random intercept and slope not supported yet

The arguments fixed_effects, random_effects, group_effects, ordered_effects and strata_effects also work when formula is not given.

meta <- data.frame(diagnosis = factor(c("CD", "UC", "nonIBD", "CD")),
                   age = c(20, 35, 50, 41),
                   subject = c("a", "a", "b", "b"))
bm_inla_formula(~ diagnosis + age + (1 | subject), meta)
#> <bm_inla_model>
#> INLA formula:
#>   y ~ 1 + diagnosis + age + f(.bm_re_subject, model = "iid", hyper = .bm_hyper$random)

Output

One row per feature, covariate level and model part:

Column Meaning
feature, metadata, value, name Feature and coefficient
coef Posterior mean
stderr Posterior standard deviation
lower_95, upper_95 95% credible interval
prob_positive Posterior probability that the effect is positive
lfsr Local false sign rate: probability that the sign of coef is wrong
qval_individual Q-value within each model part, from the selection rule
lfsr_joint, qval_joint Association in at least one of the two parts
null_hypothesis Reference the coefficient is compared with: the median across features under median comparison, otherwise 0
error Why a part was not fitted, or a warning about the estimate
model "prevalence" or "abundance"
N, N_not_zero Number of samples, and of samples where the feature is present

There are no p-values.

Selecting associations

selection turns the posteriors into qval_individual and qval_joint (and significant_results.tsv):

selection Rule
"bh_lfsr" (default) Benjamini–Hochberg on 2·lfsr within each part; joint q-value from pbeta(min(p), 1, 2) then BH
"rope" Probability that the corrected effect is practically null, P(|effect| ≤ rope_delta); q-value = running mean of the sorted probabilities
"lfsr" Running mean of the sorted lfsr (Bayesian false sign rate)

The lfsr is a sign-error probability. With continuous priors the posterior puts no mass on “no effect”, so for null features it behaves like a one-sided p-value. That is why the default applies Benjamini–Hochberg to 2·lfsr, which controls the false discovery rate, while the running-mean rules can let null features through when many features have no effect.

Main arguments

Data and model: input_data, input_metadata, output, formula, fixed_effects, random_effects, group_effects, ordered_effects, strata_effects, reference.

Filtering and pre-processing: min_abundance, min_prevalence, max_prevalence, zero_threshold, min_variance, normalization, transform, standardize.

Other: max_significance, evaluate_only, save_models, cores, verbosity.

Bayesian settings:

  • shrinkage: "joint" (default), "hierarchical" or "none"; see Sharing information across features. With evaluate_only, "hierarchical" is used instead of "joint".
  • exposure: the variable(s) of interest for "joint" (default: the first variable of the formula); the other covariates are adjustment covariates.
  • selection: "bh_lfsr" (default), "rope" or "lfsr", and rope_delta (default 0.5); see Selecting associations.
  • prior: priors, from bm_prior().
  • hierarchical_reference, hierarchical_variance, int_strategy: options of shrinkage = "hierarchical".
  • link: "none" (default) or "shared" (abundance random intercepts are a scaled copy of the prevalence ones; only with shrinkage = "none").
  • n_draws: posterior draws for the median comparison (default 4000; at most 1000 joint samples for "joint" and "hierarchical").

Median comparison: median_comparison_abundance, median_comparison_prevalence, median_comparison_abundance_threshold, median_comparison_prevalence_threshold and subtract_median.

Unsupported arguments, such as plotting or augment, are accepted but ignored, with a warning.
